core_claim.quote: Experiences of emotion and mood, which seem central to selfhood, may depend on interoceptive inferences – probabilistic best-guesses about the causes of sensory inputs signalling the physiological condition of the body

source.citation: Seth AK. Conscious artificial intelligence and biological naturalism. Behavioral and Brain Sciences 49, e315 (published online 2025-04-21)

prediction.statement: The emotion a person feels is set by the brain's predictions about the body, not by the body's signals alone, so changing what a person expects their body to be doing (for example with false heart-rate feedback) changes the emotion they feel even when the body does not change.

first_stated.passage: Extending these principles, in our model emotional content is determined by the nature of the predictive signals Ppred, and not simply by the “sensing” of interoceptive signals per se

source.citation: Seth AK, Suzuki K, Critchley HD. An interoceptive predictive coding model of conscious presence. Frontiers in Psychology 2:395 (2011 volume)

prediction.test_for: Manipulating expected bodily state (false feedback, cues) with the actual bodily state held fixed changes reported emotion in the direction of the expectation.
prediction.test_against: With the actual bodily state held fixed, manipulating expected bodily state leaves reported emotion unchanged.

other_statements_of_the_prediction.passage: In the presence component, prediction errors could be manipulated by subliminal presentation of emotive stimuli prior to target stimuli (Tamietto and de Gelder, 2010) or by false physiological feedback (Gray et al., 2007).

source.citation: Seth AK, Suzuki K, Critchley HD. An interoceptive predictive coding model of conscious presence. Frontiers in Psychology 2:395 (2011 volume)
